original.text: Systematic characterization of gesture stimuli is important for vocabulary-learning research, but human annotation is slow and costly to scale. Video-language models (VLMs) may support this process, yet their correspondence with human judgment requires empirical evaluation. We benchmarked eleven configurations from three model families (Google Gemini, OpenAI GPT, Alibaba Qwen) against 230 human raters across four language cohorts, who rated 148 instructional gesture videos on seven dimensions drawn from the Gesture Memory Support Model. Mean absolute error across configurations ranged from 0.53 to 1.12 points on five-point scales, and pooled rank correlations ranged from .62 to .69. Crucially, error and rank-order agreement dissociated: dimensions with the lowest error (enactment potential, motional salience) had the weakest or even negative rank correlations, while iconicity showed the opposite pattern. This dissociation mirrored a structural feature of the human data itself, where the same two dimensions showed the lowest interrater reliability and most compressed rating distributions. Models reliably rated mismatched gesture–word pairs lower than matched pairs, indicating genuine sensitivity to semantic compatibility, though residual ratings remained above the human floor. Cultural familiarity showed the largest model–human discrepancies; independently, human ratings on this and related dimensions varied systematically by language cohort even after controlling for item identity, indicating that the human reference itself is not culturally neutral. These findings support selective, dimension-specific use of VLMs for gesture annotation under human oversight, rather than uniform deployment across the full rating profile. The benchmark establishes correspondence with human judgment; it does not establish whether model- or human-derived ratings predict vocabulary-learning outcomes, which remains an open empirical question.

original.text: RQ2/H2 (grounded dimensions easier). H2 predicted that visually grounded dimensions (iconicity, motional salience, enactment potential) would show higher human–model agreement than culturally or affectively mediated dimensions. But enactment potential and motional salience — the dimensions H2 predicted would be easiest — had among the lowest MAEs for Gemini 3.8 Flash, essentially because human ratings on these dimensions are compressed near the scale ceiling, not because the model was tracking anything gesture-specific. On ranking (Spearman ρ), the pattern is closer to H2’s prediction, but for a more transparent reason: iconicity and sensorimotor imagery had the most consistent rank correlations, while motional salience and enactment potential — despite low error — had weak or even negative rank correlations. original.text: Cultural familiarity yielded the largest errors of any dimension across every reported configuration. Because familiarity is inherently population-dependent, a pooled human mean reflects the composition of the sampled cohorts rather than a universal property of the gesture. This is not a hypothetical concern: the video-adjusted cohort analysis reported alongside the human data found that the Japanese-language cohort rated cultural familiarity, enactment potential, and gesture complexity fit systematically lower than the German-language cohort on the identical videos, while the English-language cohort rated iconicity, motional salience, and facial-expression salience systematically lower. These are precisely the dimensions where model–human error was largest. A pooled human reference for these dimensions is therefore not a stable target, it shifts depending on which cohorts happen to be represented and in what proportion. A model score benchmarked against such a target, or later validated against a differently composed cohort, may appear to succeed or fail for reasons that have nothing to do with the model’s visual reasoning. Cohort-specific validation and transparent specification of the intended reference population are needed before ratings on these dimensions are applied in a different instructional or cultural setting.

original.text: Several extensions follow directly from the limitations above. A reliability study, repeating inference on the same items across multiple runs, prompt paraphrases, and, where available, temperature or sampling settings, would establish whether VLM ratings are stable enough to trust a single pass, which the present design cannot determine. A direct zero-shot-versus-fine-tuned comparison, using the same stimulus set and evaluation pipeline reported here, would directly address RQ4/H4, which remains open. Because cultural familiarity and several other dimensions proved population-dependent even in the human data, a deliberately cross-cultural validation design, sampling comparable numbers of raters and, ideally, comparable model prompts per language/cultural cohort — would help separate genuine model limitations from reference-target instability. A revised control-item design, in which the same gestures are evaluated under both a matched and a mismatched target word, would also let future work isolate semantic-compatibility effects from item-composition effects. Most importantly, connecting GMSM dimension scores, whether human- or model-generated, to actual vocabulary-learning outcomes in a controlled instructional study is the necessary next step before any claim about the predictive or practical value of automated gesture annotation can be made. Finally, expanding the stimulus set, refining the operational definitions to more closely track the current GMSM, and formally identifying which items function as mismatched controls in the shared data would together allow tighter confidence intervals around the dimension-specific correlations reported here and let future benchmarks track improvement in specific, currently weak dimensions such as cultural familiarity and facial-expression salience.
